title: In How Many Ways Does the Word Hide in the Text
statement:
Count the ways to pick letters of `s` (keeping their order, so you choose a set of positions) that **spell out `t`**. Two ways are different if they use different positions, even when the letters are the same. For example `rabbit` can be found in `rabbbit` in 3 ways (any one of the three `b` can be left out).

Return the number of ways. It is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit signed integer. The empty word `t` can be spelled in exactly one way (choose nothing).
constraints: s and t contain lowercase letters; the answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer

examples.explanation: The b at position 2 can pair with the a at 0 or 1 (2 ways); the b at position 5 can pair with the a at 0, 1, 3 or 4 (4 ways): 6.

hints.nudge: Look at the last letter of the word t and the last letter of the text s. If they are different, can the last letter of s be used? If they are equal, there are two things you may do with it.
hints.pattern: Dynamic programming over prefixes: ways[i][j] = number of ways to spell the first j letters of t using the first i letters of s; if s[i - 1] equals t[j - 1] you may either use that letter (ways[i - 1][j - 1]) or not (ways[i - 1][j]).
hints.walkthrough: Listing all subsequences of s is exponential. Instead count by prefixes. Spelling the first j letters of t from the first i letters of s: if the new letter s[i - 1] is not used, you get ways[i - 1][j]. It can be used only as the last letter of the spelling, i.e. when it equals t[j - 1], and then the first j - 1 letters of t must be spelled from the first i - 1 letters of s: ways[i - 1][j - 1]. Add the two cases when the letters are equal. The empty word has exactly one way for every prefix of s. With one row (updated from the right to the left so that the old values are still available) the memory is O(len(t)). Use 64-bit numbers for the table entries: intermediate values can be larger than the final answer.
